readerTitle: Your homepage has five seconds. What does it say?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (소규모 상점용 재고관리 소프트웨어 홈페이지, 동네 청소 서비스 홈페이지) · 회사명과 문구는 모두 설명용
insight: 홈페이지는 팀이 만든 것을 발표하는 곳이 아니라, 방문자의 두 질문(이게 뭐지? 나한테 맞나?)에 답하고 그다음 고객이 얻는 결과를 보여주는 곳이다.
misconception: 기능을 많이, 멋진 말로 보여줄수록 제품이 대단해 보이고 더 잘 팔린다.

sources.text: 이 유닛의 개념 레슨 MKT-04-01 (Features vs benefits), MKT-04-02 (Clarity beats cleverness)
모든 회사명, 홈페이지 문구, 고객 반응은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Shelfwise와 청소 업체, Riverside 지역명은 가상입니다. 실제 같은 이름의 회사가 있다면 혼동을 막기 위해 게시 전에 이름을 확인하거나 바꾸세요.
'5초 테스트'는 사용성 테스트에서 널리 쓰는 일반적 방법으로만 언급했습니다. 특정 연구 수치나 이탈률 통계는 일부러 넣지 않았습니다.
새 개념을 도입하지 않았는지 확인: 명확성(MKT-04-02)과 기능 대 혜택(MKT-04-01)만 사용. 고객의 말(MKT-04-03), 행동 유도(MKT-04-05)와 겹치지 않도록 했고, MKT-04-10(헤드라인 시뮬레이션)과 겹치지 않게 헤드라인 외에 기능 섹션까지 다룹니다.

cards.title: Your homepage has five seconds. What does it say?
body: Picture a small software company we'll call Shelfwise. It sells stock tracking to independent shops: hardware stores, gift shops, bike shops.
Its homepage headline reads *Inventory, reimagined.* Below it: *AI-powered, cloud-native stock management with real-time omnichannel sync.*
The founder asked five shop owners to read it. Most couldn't say what it did, or whether it was for them.

image.label: A shop owner squinting at a vague software homepage on a phone
image.brief: 작은 철물점 계산대 뒤에서 가게 주인이 휴대폰 속 홈페이지를 보며 고개를 갸웃하는 장면. 화면에는 큰 글씨 "Inventory, reimagined."만 보이고 주변에 물음표 몇 개. 실제 로고나 브랜드는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Pick the new headline.
body: You get one line at the top of the page. A shop owner has just clicked a link and will decide in seconds whether to keep reading.
Which headline should replace *Inventory, reimagined*?

options.feedback: It sounds big, but it says neither what the product is nor who it's for. That's the trap from *Clarity beats cleverness*: memorable to the writer, a riddle to the reader.

options.text: Stock tracking for independent shops. Know what's on your shelves.
options.feedback: It answers *what is this* and *is it for me* at once, then adds the payoff. Clarity first, benefit second.

options.text: Never run out of your best sellers again
options.feedback: A strong benefit. But a visitor can't tell if this is software, a supplier or a consultant. It gains appeal and loses clarity.

cards.title: Every visitor asks two silent questions.
body: A homepage visitor arrives asking *What is this?* and *Is it for me?* A clever line makes them work for the answer. Busy people usually don't.
That's **clarity beats cleverness** at work. *Inventory, reimagined* felt bold to the team that wrote it. To a shop owner between customers, it said nothing they could use.
Clear doesn't mean dull. It means the answer comes before the style.

cards.title: Now fix the first feature.
body: Under the headline, the old page lists features. The first one reads: *Automated reorder points with configurable thresholds.*
What should that line say instead?

options.feedback: Shorter, but it's still a feature with a buzzword on top. The shop owner still has to guess what it does for them.

options.text: Get a text before a best seller runs out
options.feedback: This is **features vs benefits**: the same function, described as the result the owner feels. Keep the feature name in smaller type for people comparing tools.

options.text: Set a minimum stock level for every product
options.feedback: Much clearer, and some owners want exactly this control. But it describes the tool's work, not the owner's win.

cards.title: Ask every feature: so what?
body: Go down the list and ask of each line: *what does the shop owner actually get?*
list: **Real-time omnichannel sync** → Sell online and in store without selling the same item twice
**Mobile barcode scanning** → Count stock with your phone. No scanner to buy
**Supplier purchase orders** → Reorder from your suppliers without retyping lists
**Sales analytics dashboard** → See which products earn their shelf space
cards.callout: Lead with the benefit. Keep the feature underneath as proof.

cards.title: Same product. Different page.
body: Nothing about the software changed. The old page described what the team built. The new one describes what a shop owner gets, in plain words.
The headline now says what it is and who it's for. Each feature now starts with a result someone can picture. The page reads like an answer, not an announcement.

image.label: Side-by-side homepage, before and after the rewrite
image.brief: 홈페이지 두 개를 나란히 배치. 왼쪽(Before)은 "Inventory, reimagined."와 전문용어 기능 목록, 흐릿한 회색 톤. 오른쪽(After)은 "Stock tracking for independent shops" 헤드라인과 "Get a text before a best seller runs out" 같은 혜택 문장, 밝은 톤. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Benefits can go vague too.
body: *Save time* and *Grow your business* are benefits, but every competitor can say them. A useful benefit is specific enough to picture, like a text before stock runs out.
Some buyers, such as a chain's operations manager, compare feature lists line by line. Don't delete the details. Move them lower on the page.
And test before you trust your rewrite. Show the page to a real customer for five seconds, hide it, and ask what the product does.

cards.title: Now it's a house-cleaning company.
body: A local cleaning business's homepage says: *Where clean meets care.* Below it: *Eco-certified products. Insured, vetted staff. Flexible scheduling.*
Which rewrite of the top of the page works hardest?

options.feedback: Still a riddle. It could be a hotel, a laundry or a soap brand. It keeps the polish and loses the clarity.

options.text: House cleaning in Riverside. Come home to a clean house, booked online in a minute.
options.feedback: Clear on what, where and for whom, then a benefit you can picture. Both ideas at work: **clarity** and **benefits over features**.

options.text: Insured, vetted, eco-friendly cleaners you can trust
options.feedback: Clear and reassuring, and these details matter to customers letting strangers into their home. But they're features. They work best as proof just below a benefit headline.

cards.softwareNote: The same rewrite works for any page: an app store listing, a pricing page, a sales deck's first slide. Say what it is, then what the customer gets.

cards.title: Say what it is. Then say what they get.
body: This lesson used two ideas. **Clarity beats cleverness:** answer *what is this* and *is it for me* first. **Features vs benefits:** turn each feature into a result the customer feels, and keep the feature as proof.
**Try it today:** show your homepage or flyer to someone outside your business for five seconds. Then ask what you sell and who it's for.
